Processing in the Brain","kind":"detailed_source_grounded_notes","printedStart":161,"printedEnd":175,"pdfStart":179,"pdfEnd":193,"content":[{"type":"paragraph","text":"Visual signals are transformed at several stages between the retina and cerebral cortex. Retinal processing, receptive fields, and cortical responses help explain how the brain extracts useful visual features."},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The development of visual cortex also depends on early experience. Read the deprivation findings as evidence about sensitive periods and neural wiring rather than as a claim that sight is a passive recording of the world."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m5-2-study-1","text":"The route from eye to cortex"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Visual information leaves the retina through retinal ganglion cell axons and travels through central pathways that include the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus and primary visual cortex. Signals from the two eyes are organized so the brain can combine information about space while preserving important distinctions. Processing already occurs in retinal circuits and continues through interconnected cortical regions. A complete explanation needs both the pathway and the transformations performed along it."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m5-2-study-2","text":"Receptive fields and edge processing"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A receptive field is the region of sensory space in which stimulation affects a neuron's activity. Retinal and thalamic cells often respond to patterns such as differences between center and surrounding light, allowing the system to emphasize contrast. In visual cortex, some cells respond best to oriented edges or combinations of features. The 'feature detector' label is useful but incomplete: responses depend on context, networks, and past experience. Recognition cannot be explained by stacking isolated detectors without understanding their interactions."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m5-2-study-3","text":"How experience shapes visual cortex"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Early visual experience helps organize cortical circuits. Restricted input to one eye, both eyes, or particular patterns can alter later responses; the outcome depends on the age and duration of the deprivation. Binocular cooperation depends partly on correlated visual stimulation. These findings are important for understanding why some visual problems in infancy need attention early, while also showing that visual development involves more than genetically fixed wiring."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m5-2-study-4","text":"From local responses to perception"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Seeing an object requires processing contours, color, motion, and spatial relations across many neuronal populations. The visual cortex has specialized response properties, yet its function rests on a network of feedforward and feedback connections. A diagram of the pathway tells you where information travels; receptive-field experiments tell you what particular populations respond to. Neither kind of evidence alone fully explains conscious visual experience."},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m5-2-h01","text":"An Overview of the Mammalian Visual System"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The horizontal cells make inhibitory contact onto bipolar cells, which in turn make synapses onto amacrine cells and ganglion cells.","sourcePrintedPage":161,"sourcePdfPage":179,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"There, in humans, half the axons from each eye cross to the opposite side of the brain.","sourcePrintedPage":161,"sourcePdfPage":179,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Information from the temporal half (the side toward the temporal cortex) goes to the ipsilateral hemisphere.","sourcePrintedPage":161,"sourcePdfPage":179,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The percentage of crossover varies from one species to another depending on the location of the eyes.","sourcePrintedPage":161,"sourcePdfPage":179,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In species with eyes far to the sides of the head, such as rabbits and guinea pigs, most axons cross to the opposite side.","sourcePrintedPage":161,"sourcePdfPage":179,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The shape of the lateral geniculate must have looked like a knee to some early anatomist.) Other axons go from the eye to the superior colliculus (important for eye movements, among other functions) and to the part of the hypothalamus that controls the waking– sleeping schedule.","sourcePrintedPage":162,"sourcePdfPage":180,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The lateral geniculate sends input to other parts of the thalamus and to the visual cortex.","sourcePrintedPage":162,"sourcePdfPage":180,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m5-2-h02","text":"Processing in the Retina"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Lateral inhibition is the retina’s way of sharpening contrasts to emphasize the borders of objects.","sourcePrintedPage":162,"sourcePdfPage":180,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The result is a sharp contrast at the border between those receiving cookies and those not.","sourcePrintedPage":162,"sourcePdfPage":180,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The analogy may sound silly—okay, it is silly—but it illustrates what happens in the retina.","sourcePrintedPage":162,"sourcePdfPage":180,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Actually, light striking the rods and cones decreases their spontaneous output, and the receptors make inhibitory synapses onto the bipolar cells.","sourcePrintedPage":162,"sourcePdfPage":180,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"It also excites a horizontal cell that inhibits bipolar cells, especially the closest ones, as depicted by red arrows.","sourcePrintedPage":163,"sourcePdfPage":181,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Bipolar cell 8 has net excitation, because the excitatory synapse outweighs the effect of the horizontal cell’s inhibition. (It’s like gaining cookies and then losing a smaller number.) The bipolar cells to the sides (laterally) get no excitation but some inhibition.","sourcePrintedPage":163,"sourcePdfPage":181,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Bipolar cells 7, 8, and 9 are inhibited by input on both sides, but bipolar cells 6 and 10 are inhibited from only one side, and therefore 6 and 10 respond the most.","sourcePrintedPage":163,"sourcePdfPage":181,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Bipolar cells 5 and 11 receive no excitation, but the horizontal cell inhibits them.","sourcePrintedPage":163,"sourcePdfPage":181,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"These results illustrate lateral inhibition , reduced activity in a neuron because of activity in neighboring neurons .","sourcePrintedPage":163,"sourcePdfPage":181,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m5-2-h03","text":"Further Processing"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Each cell in the visual system of the brain has a receptive field , an area in visual space from which light excites or inhibits the cell.","sourcePrintedPage":163,"sourcePdfPage":181,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The receptive field of a rod or cone is the point in space from which light strikes the cell.","sourcePrintedPage":163,"sourcePdfPage":181,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Everyone on the street reports to a supervisor, whose receptive field is the whole street, the combined area of input.","sourcePrintedPage":163,"sourcePdfPage":181,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"All the street supervisors report to the neighborhood manager, whose receptive field is the whole neighborhood.","sourcePrintedPage":163,"sourcePdfPage":181,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Rods and cones with tiny receptive fields connect to a bipolar cell, with a receptive field that combines those of all cells connected to it,","sourcePrintedPage":163,"sourcePdfPage":181,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The receptive fields of ganglion cells converge at the next level, and so on.","sourcePrintedPage":164,"sourcePdfPage":182,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"To find a cell’s receptive field, an investigator records from the cell while shining light in various locations.","sourcePrintedPage":164,"sourcePdfPage":182,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"If light on a particular spot excites or inhibits the neuron, then that location is part of the neuron’s excitatory or inhibitory receptive field.","sourcePrintedPage":164,"sourcePdfPage":182,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In the simplest case, a ganglion cell’s receptive field has a circular center and an antagonistic doughnutshaped surround.","sourcePrintedPage":164,"sourcePdfPage":182,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The magnocellular neurons, with larger receptive fields, respond to movement and overall patterns, but not color or fine details.","sourcePrintedPage":165,"sourcePdfPage":183,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m5-2-h04","text":"The Primary Visual Cortex"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Information goes from the ganglion cells to the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus and then to the primary visual cortex in the occipital cortex, also known","sourcePrintedPage":165,"sourcePdfPage":183,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"as area V1 or the striate cortex because of its striped appearance.","sourcePrintedPage":165,"sourcePdfPage":183,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Activity from V1 projects to the frontal cortex, which within 100–200 milliseconds sends information back to modify the activity in V1 and other visual areas.","sourcePrintedPage":165,"sourcePdfPage":183,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"People with damage in and around area V1 report no conscious vision, no visual imagery, and no visual dreams .","sourcePrintedPage":165,"sourcePdfPage":183,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"About 1 to 3 percent of people have no visual imagery at all, other than maybe in a dream now and then.","sourcePrintedPage":165,"sourcePdfPage":183,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"People with this condition, called aphantasia , tend to be attracted toward math and science.","sourcePrintedPage":165,"sourcePdfPage":183,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Some people with damage to area V1 display a surprising phenomenon called blindsight , the ability to respond to visual information without perceiving it consciously.","sourcePrintedPage":165,"sourcePdfPage":183,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Many patients respond in one of these ways and not the others, because of differences in which connections were damaged.","sourcePrintedPage":165,"sourcePdfPage":183,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In one study, every patient with blindsight had intact connections from the visual area of the thalamus to the temporal cortex .","sourcePrintedPage":166,"sourcePdfPage":184,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m5-2-h05","text":"Simple and Complex Receptive Fields"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In the 1950s, David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel inserted thin electrodes to record activity from cells in cats’ and monkeys’ occipital cortex while they presented visual patterns to the retina.","sourcePrintedPage":166,"sourcePdfPage":184,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The cell had a bar-shaped receptive field, rather than a circular receptive field like cells in the retina and lateral geniculate .","sourcePrintedPage":166,"sourcePdfPage":184,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Light in the excitatory zone increases responses and light in the inhibitory zone decreases it.","sourcePrintedPage":166,"sourcePdfPage":184,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Most simple cells have bar-shaped or edge-shaped receptive fields in horizontal or vertical orientations.","sourcePrintedPage":166,"sourcePdfPage":184,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Most complex cells respond mostly to a stimulus moving in a particular direction—for example, a vertical bar moving left to right.","sourcePrintedPage":166,"sourcePdfPage":184,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The best way to classify a cell as simple or complex is to present a stimulus in several locations.","sourcePrintedPage":166,"sourcePdfPage":184,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A cell that responds to a stimulus in only one location is a simple cell.","sourcePrintedPage":166,"sourcePdfPage":184,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Later researchers found that a cortical cell that responds well to a single bar or line","sourcePrintedPage":167,"sourcePdfPage":185,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Many cortical neurons respond best to a particular spatial frequency of lines and hardly at all to other frequencies .","sourcePrintedPage":168,"sourcePdfPage":186,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"How the brain codes vision does not match what we see in any very simple way.","sourcePrintedPage":168,"sourcePdfPage":186,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m5-2-h06","text":"Are Visual Cortex Cells Feature Detectors?"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Given that neurons in area V1 respond strongly to particular patterns, we might suppose that the activity of such a cell represents the perception of that pattern, such as lines or bars.","sourcePrintedPage":168,"sourcePdfPage":186,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"If so, such cells would be feature detectors —neurons whose responses indicate the presence of a particular feature.","sourcePrintedPage":168,"sourcePdfPage":186,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Supporting the idea of feature detectors is the fact that prolonged exposure to a given visual feature decreases sensitivity to that feature, as if it fatigued the relevant detectors.","sourcePrintedPage":168,"sourcePdfPage":186,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Long ago, Gestalt psychologists rejected the idea that feature detectors tell the whole story about our perceptions.","sourcePrintedPage":168,"sourcePdfPage":186,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"It is a top-down process in which other brain areas interpret the visual stimulus and send messages back to reorganize V1 activity.","sourcePrintedPage":168,"sourcePdfPage":186,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In a sense, the brain is constantly forming hypotheses or expectations about the world, and then modifying them based on “prediction errors” when it compares the expectations to sensory input .","sourcePrintedPage":168,"sourcePdfPage":186,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m5-2-h07","text":"Development of the Visual Cortex"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Then, for the first time, you came out into the light and looked around.","sourcePrintedPage":169,"sourcePdfPage":187,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Within months, however, you began to recognize faces and crawl toward your favorite toys.","sourcePrintedPage":169,"sourcePdfPage":187,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In a newborn mammal, many properties of the visual system develop before birth .","sourcePrintedPage":169,"sourcePdfPage":187,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Waves of spontaneous activity sweep over the developing retina, synchronizing the activity of neighboring receptors and enabling appropriate combinations of receptors to establish connections with cells in the brain .","sourcePrintedPage":169,"sourcePdfPage":187,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A study of people who were born without eyes found that the connections from the primary visual cortex to its main targets were more or less normal .","sourcePrintedPage":169,"sourcePdfPage":187,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Nevertheless, visual experience after birth is necessary for maintaining and modifying the connections.","sourcePrintedPage":169,"sourcePdfPage":187,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m5-2-h08","text":"Deprived Experience in One Eye"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"When a kitten opens its eyes at about age 9 days, each neuron responds to areas in the two retinas that focus on approximately the same point in space—a process necessary for binocular vision.","sourcePrintedPage":169,"sourcePdfPage":187,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"right because the exact distance between the eyes varies from one kitten to another, and the distance changes over age.","sourcePrintedPage":169,"sourcePdfPage":187,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"If an experimenter sutures one eyelid shut for a kitten’s first 4 to 6 weeks of life, synapses in the visual cortex gradually become unresponsive to input from the deprived eye .","sourcePrintedPage":169,"sourcePdfPage":187,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"After an eye deprived of vision in adults is reopened, cells gradually return to their previous levels of responsiveness .","sourcePrintedPage":169,"sourcePdfPage":187,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m5-2-h09","text":"Deprived Experience in Both Eyes"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"You might guess that the kitten would become insensitive to both eyes, but it does not.","sourcePrintedPage":169,"sourcePdfPage":187,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"When just one eye is open, the synapses from the open eye release a chemical that inhibits the synapses from the closed eye .","sourcePrintedPage":169,"sourcePdfPage":187,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"For at least 3 weeks, the kitten’s cortex remains responsive to visual input, although most cells become responsive to just one eye or the other and not both .","sourcePrintedPage":169,"sourcePdfPage":187,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"If the eyes remain shut still longer, the cortical responses start to become sluggish and lose their well-defined receptive fields .","sourcePrintedPage":169,"sourcePdfPage":187,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"For each aspect of visual experience, researchers identify a sensitive period , when experiences have a particularly strong and enduring influence .","sourcePrintedPage":169,"sourcePdfPage":187,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"infant into an older mouse could induce a new period of heightened susceptibility to experience .","sourcePrintedPage":170,"sourcePdfPage":188,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, even long after the sensitive period, a prolonged experience—such as a full week without visual stimulation to one eye—produces a smaller but measurable effect on the visual cortex .","sourcePrintedPage":170,"sourcePdfPage":188,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m5-2-h10","text":"Uncorrelated Stimulation in the Two Eyes"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Stereoscopic depth perception requires the brain to detect retinal disparity , the discrepancy between what the left and right eyes see.","sourcePrintedPage":170,"sourcePdfPage":188,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"During early development, each neuron in the visual cortex receives many inputs from both eyes, but it uses inhibitory synapses to suppress unmatching inputs.","sourcePrintedPage":170,"sourcePdfPage":188,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The result is to make the neuron responsive to corresponding areas of the left and right eyes—areas that see the same thing at the same time .","sourcePrintedPage":170,"sourcePdfPage":188,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A neuron that cannot find matching input from the two eyes will become responsive to just one eye or the other .","sourcePrintedPage":170,"sourcePdfPage":188,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Both eyes are active, but no cortical neuron consistently receives matching messages from the two eyes.","sourcePrintedPage":170,"sourcePdfPage":188,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Therefore, almost every neuron in the visual cortex becomes responsive to just one eye or the other .","sourcePrintedPage":170,"sourcePdfPage":188,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"That procedure increases attention to the ignored eye, especially if it begins early , but many children refuse to wear an eye patch for long enough.","sourcePrintedPage":170,"sourcePdfPage":188,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m5-2-h11","text":"Early Exposure to a Limited Array of Patterns"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"If a kitten spends its entire early sensitive period wearing goggles with horizontal lines painted on them (Figure 5.23), nearly all its visual cortex cells become responsive only to horizontal lines .","sourcePrintedPage":170,"sourcePdfPage":188,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Even after months of later normal experience, the cat does not respond to vertical lines .","sourcePrintedPage":170,"sourcePdfPage":188,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"They become more sensitive to the kind of line they have seen.","sourcePrintedPage":170,"sourcePdfPage":188,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"their child to such a procedure, and it never happens in nature.","sourcePrintedPage":171,"sourcePdfPage":189,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"About 70 percent of all infants have astigmatism , a blurring of vision for lines in one direction (e.g., horizontal, vertical, or one of the diagonals), caused by an asymmetric curvature of the eyes.","sourcePrintedPage":171,"sourcePdfPage":189,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Normal growth reduces the prevalence of astigmatism to about 10 percent in 4-year-old children.","sourcePrintedPage":171,"sourcePdfPage":189,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"If so, rotate the page to demonstrate that the darkness is in you, not in the lines themselves.","sourcePrintedPage":171,"sourcePdfPage":189,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"appearance of the lines depends on their position.","sourcePrintedPage":171,"sourcePdfPage":189,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m5-2-h12","text":"Impaired Infant Vision and Long-Term Consequences"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In some countries, a newborn with dense cataracts (cloudy spots on the lenses that prevent perception of anything other than bright versus dark) may have to wait years for surgery to enable vision.","sourcePrintedPage":171,"sourcePdfPage":189,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"When the cataracts are finally removed, researchers can examine what happened to vision after years of almost total deprivation.","sourcePrintedPage":171,"sourcePdfPage":189,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In one study, children looked at a picture of a toy block, and another picture with two blocks.","sourcePrintedPage":171,"sourcePdfPage":189,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The task was to point to the block in the second picture that matched the first.","sourcePrintedPage":171,"sourcePdfPage":189,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, when the task was to feel a block and point to which of two choices was the picture of that block, the children’s performance was only a little better than chance.","sourcePrintedPage":171,"sourcePdfPage":189,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Seeing well enough to ride a bicycle took a year and a half .","sourcePrintedPage":171,"sourcePdfPage":189,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Some aspects of vision, such as motion perception and depth perception, never reached normal levels .","sourcePrintedPage":171,"sourcePdfPage":189,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A study of another group of children who had binocular cataracts surgically repaired at ages 6 to 11 reported much variation in their development.","sourcePrintedPage":171,"sourcePdfPage":189,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Eventually he learned to recognize common household objects, but unlike most people who identify objects immediately, he had to think about it carefully .","sourcePrintedPage":171,"sourcePdfPage":189,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m5-2-h13","text":"In Closing: Understanding Vision by Understanding the Wiring Diagram"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The nervous system from the start identifies the borders between one object and another by lateral inhibition.","sourcePrintedPage":172,"sourcePdfPage":190,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"It identifies lines and their locations by simple and complex cells in the primary visual cortex.","sourcePrintedPage":172,"sourcePdfPage":190,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Researchers have gone a long way toward mapping out the excitatory and inhibitory connections that make these cells possible.","sourcePrintedPage":172,"sourcePdfPage":190,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"While he was blind, he had learned to ski by following verbal directions and memorizing hills.","sourcePrintedPage":172,"sourcePdfPage":190,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Two years later he could use vision to estimate the steepness of a hill, and he was willing to open his eyes while skiing, but only on relatively easy slopes.","sourcePrintedPage":172,"sourcePdfPage":190,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Evidently, the visual understanding that most of us take for granted depends on practice early in life.","sourcePrintedPage":172,"sourcePdfPage":190,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"bullet","text":"Let’s begin with the anatomy of the mammalian visual system.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h01","sourcePrintedPage":161,"sourcePdfPage":179},{"type":"bullet","text":"The rods and cones of the retina make synapses with horizontal cells and bipolar cells (Figures 5.3 and 5.14).","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h01","sourcePrintedPage":161,"sourcePdfPage":179},{"type":"bullet","text":"Most of the optic nerve goes to the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h01","sourcePrintedPage":161,"sourcePdfPage":179},{"type":"bullet","text":"Axons from the cortex go back to the thalamus to modify thalamic activity.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h01","sourcePrintedPage":162,"sourcePdfPage":180},{"type":"bullet","text":"Here is an analogy to demonstrate how it works: Suppose people stand in a line, each holding one cookie.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h02","sourcePrintedPage":162,"sourcePdfPage":180},{"type":"bullet","text":"Someone hands 5 extra cookies to the 5 people in the middle of the line, but then each of those 5 people has to throw away one of their own cookies, and one cookie from each of their neighbors.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h02","sourcePrintedPage":162,"sourcePdfPage":180},{"type":"bullet","text":"You don’t want to be in the middle of the cookie-receiving group, because after gaining 5 you would have to throw away one of your own and lose one to each of your neighbors.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h02","sourcePrintedPage":162,"sourcePdfPage":180},{"type":"bullet","text":"Decreased inhibition means net excitation, so to avoid double negatives, let’s think of the receptors’ output as excitation of the bipolar cells.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h02","sourcePrintedPage":162,"sourcePdfPage":180},{"type":"bullet","text":"In this diagram, the thickness of the arrow indicates the amount of excitation or inhibition.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h02","sourcePrintedPage":163,"sourcePdfPage":181},{"type":"bullet","text":"In olfaction, a strong stimulus uses lateral inhibition to suppress the response to one that follows slightly after it.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h02","sourcePrintedPage":163,"sourcePdfPage":181},{"type":"bullet","text":"Other visual cells derive their receptive fields from the connections they receive.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h03","sourcePrintedPage":163,"sourcePdfPage":181},{"type":"bullet","text":"For analogy, suppose you keep track of events on a city block.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h03","sourcePrintedPage":163,"sourcePdfPage":181},{"type":"bullet","text":"Bipolar cells report to a ganglion cell, which therefore has a larger receptive field, as illustrated in Figure 5.17.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h03","sourcePrintedPage":164,"sourcePdfPage":182},{"type":"bullet","text":"The receptive field might be excited by light in the center and inhibited by light in the surround, or the opposite.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h03","sourcePrintedPage":164,"sourcePdfPage":182},{"type":"bullet","text":"Some ganglion cells respond only to a stimulus moving in a particular direction.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h03","sourcePrintedPage":164,"sourcePdfPage":182},{"type":"bullet","text":"(Parvocellular means “small celled,” from the Latin root parv, meaning “small.”) Magnocellular neurons, with larger cell bodies and receptive fields, are distributed evenly throughout the retina.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h03","sourcePrintedPage":165,"sourcePdfPage":183},{"type":"bullet","text":"(Magnocellular means “large celled,” from the Latin root magn, meaning “large,” as in the word magnify.) The koniocellular neurons have small cell bodies, like the parvocellular neurons, but they occur throughout the retina.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h03","sourcePrintedPage":165,"sourcePdfPage":183},{"type":"bullet","text":"Hyperphantasia is more common among women than men, and it tends to be associated with artistic and other creative occupations.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h04","sourcePrintedPage":165,"sourcePdfPage":183},{"type":"bullet","text":"When you imagine a visual scene, the activity starts in the memory and language areas of the cortex, and then spreads gradually to V1.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h04","sourcePrintedPage":165,"sourcePdfPage":183},{"type":"bullet","text":"In any case, the conclusion remains that V1 and surrounding areas are essential for conscious vision.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h04","sourcePrintedPage":166,"sourcePdfPage":184},{"type":"bullet","text":"Even if your brain is intact, you could experience something like blindsight under certain circumstances.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h04","sourcePrintedPage":166,"sourcePdfPage":184},{"type":"bullet","text":"The illustration shows the receptive field of a simple cell.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h05","sourcePrintedPage":166,"sourcePdfPage":184},{"type":"bullet","text":"A simple cell has a receptive field with fixed excitatory and inhibitory zones.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h05","sourcePrintedPage":166,"sourcePdfPage":184},{"type":"bullet","text":"Complex cells, located in areas V1 and V2, also respond to bars and edges, but they respond equally anywhere within a large receptive field.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h05","sourcePrintedPage":166,"sourcePdfPage":184},{"type":"bullet","text":"An end-stopped or hypercomplex cell resembles a complex cell except that it has a strong inhibitory area at one end of its bar-shaped receptive field.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h05","sourcePrintedPage":166,"sourcePdfPage":184},{"type":"bullet","text":"From a mathematical standpoint, sine wave frequencies are easy to work with.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h05","sourcePrintedPage":168,"sourcePdfPage":186},{"type":"bullet","text":"A branch of mathematics called Fourier analysis demonstrates that a combination of sine waves can produce an unlimited variety of other patterns.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h05","sourcePrintedPage":168,"sourcePdfPage":186},{"type":"bullet","text":"Thus, a series of spatial frequency detectors, some sensitive to horizontal patterns and others to vertical patterns, could represent any possible display.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h05","sourcePrintedPage":168,"sourcePdfPage":186},{"type":"bullet","text":"Still, we perceive the world as objects, not sine waves.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h05","sourcePrintedPage":168,"sourcePdfPage":186},{"type":"bullet","text":"For example, if you stare at a waterfall for a minute or more and then look away, the rocks and trees next to the waterfall appear to flow upward.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h06","sourcePrintedPage":168,"sourcePdfPage":186},{"type":"bullet","text":"For example, if you examine Figure 5.22, you might at first see nothing.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h06","sourcePrintedPage":168,"sourcePdfPage":186},{"type":"bullet","text":"Unless you were born blind, you did have this experience—on the day you were born!","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h07","sourcePrintedPage":169,"sourcePdfPage":187},{"type":"bullet","text":"The young of mammals such as horses have to make sense of vision quickly, as they start walking and following their mother shortly after birth.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h07","sourcePrintedPage":169,"sourcePdfPage":187},{"type":"bullet","text":"After the deprived eye is opened, the kitten does not respond to it.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h08","sourcePrintedPage":169,"sourcePdfPage":187},{"type":"bullet","text":"A similar period of deprivation in older animals weakens the response to the deprived eye, but not as strongly as it does in young ones.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h08","sourcePrintedPage":169,"sourcePdfPage":187},{"type":"bullet","text":"If neither eye is active, no axon outcompetes any other.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h09","sourcePrintedPage":169,"sourcePdfPage":187},{"type":"bullet","text":"Eventually, the visual cortex may start responding to auditory or touch stimuli instead.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h09","sourcePrintedPage":169,"sourcePdfPage":187},{"type":"bullet","text":"Cortical plasticity is greatest in early life, but it never ends.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h09","sourcePrintedPage":170,"sourcePdfPage":188},{"type":"bullet","text":"Certain children are born with strabismus (or strabismic amblyopia), also known as “lazy eye,” a condition in which the eyes do not point in the same direction.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h10","sourcePrintedPage":170,"sourcePdfPage":188},{"type":"bullet","text":"In any case, the procedure does not prompt the child to use both eyes at the same time.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h10","sourcePrintedPage":170,"sourcePdfPage":188},{"type":"bullet","text":"You can informally test yourself for astigmatism with Figure 5.24.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h11","sourcePrintedPage":171,"sourcePdfPage":189},{"type":"bullet","text":"If you wear corrective lenses, try this demonstration with and without them.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h11","sourcePrintedPage":171,"sourcePdfPage":189},{"type":"bullet","text":"If you see a difference in the lines only without your lenses, then the lenses have corrected your astigmatism.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h11","sourcePrintedPage":171,"sourcePdfPage":189},{"type":"bullet","text":"At the start of this section, we raised the question of what you would see if you lived all your life in the dark and then suddenly could see.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h12","sourcePrintedPage":171,"sourcePdfPage":189},{"type":"bullet","text":"One man had normal vision in early childhood until age 31⁄2, when a chemical explosion destroyed one eye and damaged the cornea of his other eye so badly that he could see nothing more than light vs. dark.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h12","sourcePrintedPage":171,"sourcePdfPage":189},{"type":"bullet","text":"Your eyes are bombarded with a complex pattern of light emanating from every source in front of you.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h13","sourcePrintedPage":172,"sourcePdfPage":190},{"type":"bullet","text":"Out of all this, your brain needs to extract the most useful information.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h13","sourcePrintedPage":172,"sourcePdfPage":190},{"type":"bullet","text":"When he tried skiing with his eyes open, the result was frightening.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h13","sourcePrintedPage":172,"sourcePdfPage":190},{"type":"bullet","text":"On the most difficult hills, he insisted on closing his eyes!","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h13","sourcePrintedPage":172,"sourcePdfPage":190},{"type":"bullet","text":"After a receptor cell is stimulated, the bipolar cell receiving input from it demonstrates an immediate strong response.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h13","sourcePrintedPage":173,"sourcePdfPage":191},{"type":"bullet","text":"A fraction of a second later, the bipolar’s response decreases, even though the stimulation from the receptor cell remains constant.","headingId":"bp14-m5-2-h13","sourcePrintedPage":173,"sourcePdfPage":191}],"topicIds":["bp14-m5-2-h01","bp14-m5-2-h02","bp14-m5-2-h03","bp14-m5-2-h04","bp14-m5-2-h05","bp14-m5-2-h06","bp14-m5-2-h07","bp14-m5-2-h08","bp14-m5-2-h09","bp14-m5-2-h10","bp14-m5-2-h11","bp14-m5-2-h12","bp14-m5-2-h13"],"studySections":[{"id":"bp14-m5-2-study-1","title":"The route from eye to cortex","text":"Visual information leaves the retina through retinal ganglion cell axons and travels through central pathways that include the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus and primary visual cortex. Signals from the two eyes are organized so the brain can combine information about space while preserving important distinctions. Processing already occurs in retinal circuits and continues through interconnected cortical regions. A complete explanation needs both the pathway and the transformations performed along it.","kind":"companion_original_explanation","sourcePrintedStart":161,"sourcePrintedEnd":175,"sourcePdfStart":179,"sourcePdfEnd":193},{"id":"bp14-m5-2-study-2","title":"Receptive fields and edge processing","text":"A receptive field is the region of sensory space in which stimulation affects a neuron's activity. Retinal and thalamic cells often respond to patterns such as differences between center and surrounding light, allowing the system to emphasize contrast. In visual cortex, some cells respond best to oriented edges or combinations of features. The 'feature detector' label is useful but incomplete: responses depend on context, networks, and past experience. Recognition cannot be explained by stacking isolated detectors without understanding their interactions.","kind":"companion_original_explanation","sourcePrintedStart":161,"sourcePrintedEnd":175,"sourcePdfStart":179,"sourcePdfEnd":193},{"id":"bp14-m5-2-study-3","title":"How experience shapes visual cortex","text":"Early visual experience helps organize cortical circuits. Restricted input to one eye, both eyes, or particular patterns can alter later responses; the outcome depends on the age and duration of the deprivation. Binocular cooperation depends partly on correlated visual stimulation. These findings are important for understanding why some visual problems in infancy need attention early, while also showing that visual development involves more than genetically fixed wiring.","kind":"companion_original_explanation","sourcePrintedStart":161,"sourcePrintedEnd":175,"sourcePdfStart":179,"sourcePdfEnd":193},{"id":"bp14-m5-2-study-4","title":"From local responses to perception","text":"Seeing an object requires processing contours, color, motion, and spatial relations across many neuronal populations. The visual cortex has specialized response properties, yet its function rests on a network of feedforward and feedback connections. A diagram of the pathway tells you where information travels; receptive-field experiments tell you what particular populations respond to. Neither kind of evidence alone fully explains conscious visual experience.","kind":"companion_original_explanation","sourcePrintedStart":161,"sourcePrintedEnd":175,"sourcePdfStart":179,"sourcePdfEnd":193}],"contentLevel":"verified_hierarchical_topic_notes_and_module_explanations","selfCheck":[{"question":"Can you explain: The route from eye to cortex?","answer":"Visual information leaves the retina through retinal ganglion cell axons and travels through central pathways that include the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus and primary visual cortex. Neither kind of evidence alone fully explains conscious visual experience."}],"deepContentStart":10,"deepTopics":[{"id":"bp14-m5-2-h01","title":"An Overview of the Mammalian Visual System","level":1,"printedPage":161,"pdfPage":179,"parentId":null,"status":"detailed","extractionMethod":"pdf_extract_selected_sentences","mdHeadingCrosscheck":"terms_present","facts":[{"text":"The horizontal cells make inhibitory contact onto bipolar cells, which in turn make synapses onto amacrine cells and ganglion cells.","printedPage":161,"pdfPage":179,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":11},{"text":"There, in humans, half the axons from each eye cross to the opposite side of the brain.","printedPage":161,"pdfPage":179,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":12},{"text":"Information from the temporal half (the side toward the temporal cortex) goes to the ipsilateral hemisphere.","printedPage":161,"pdfPage":179,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":13},{"text":"The percentage of crossover varies from one species to another depending on the location of the eyes.","printedPage":161,"pdfPage":179,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":14},{"text":"In species with eyes far to the sides of the head, such as rabbits and guinea pigs, most axons cross to the opposite side.","printedPage":161,"pdfPage":179,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":15},{"text":"The shape of the lateral geniculate must have looked like a knee to some early anatomist.) Other axons go from the eye to the superior colliculus (important for eye movements, among other functions) and to the part of the hypothalamus that controls the waking– sleeping schedule.","printedPage":162,"pdfPage":180,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":16},{"text":"The lateral geniculate sends input to other parts of the thalamus and to the visual cortex.","printedPage":162,"pdfPage":180,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":17}],"sourceWordCount":303},{"id":"bp14-m5-2-h02","title":"Processing in the Retina","level":1,"printedPage":162,"pdfPage":180,"parentId":null,"status":"detailed","extractionMethod":"pdf_extract_selected_sentences","mdHeadingCrosscheck":"terms_present","facts":[{"text":"Lateral inhibition is the retina’s way of sharpening contrasts to emphasize the borders of objects.","printedPage":162,"pdfPage":180,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":19},{"text":"The result is a sharp contrast at the border between those receiving cookies and those not.","printedPage":162,"pdfPage":180,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":20},{"text":"The analogy may sound silly—okay, it is silly—but it illustrates what happens in the retina.","printedPage":162,"pdfPage":180,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":21},{"text":"Actually, light striking the rods and cones decreases their spontaneous output, and the receptors make inhibitory synapses onto the bipolar cells.","printedPage":162,"pdfPage":180,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":22},{"text":"It also excites a horizontal cell that inhibits bipolar cells, especially the closest ones, as depicted by red arrows.","printedPage":163,"pdfPage":181,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":23},{"text":"Bipolar cell 8 has net excitation, because the excitatory synapse outweighs the effect of the horizontal cell’s inhibition. (It’s like gaining cookies and then losing a smaller number.) The bipolar cells to the sides (laterally) get no excitation but some inhibition.","printedPage":163,"pdfPage":181,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":24},{"text":"Bipolar cells 7, 8, and 9 are inhibited by input on both sides, but bipolar cells 6 and 10 are inhibited from only one side, and therefore 6 and 10 respond the most.","printedPage":163,"pdfPage":181,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":25},{"text":"Bipolar cells 5 and 11 receive no excitation, but the horizontal cell inhibits them.","printedPage":163,"pdfPage":181,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":26},{"text":"These results illustrate lateral inhibition , reduced activity in a neuron because of activity in neighboring neurons .","printedPage":163,"pdfPage":181,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":27}],"sourceWordCount":626},{"id":"bp14-m5-2-h03","title":"Further Processing","level":1,"printedPage":163,"pdfPage":181,"parentId":null,"status":"detailed","extractionMethod":"pdf_extract_selected_sentences","mdHeadingCrosscheck":"terms_present","facts":[{"text":"Each cell in the visual system of the brain has a receptive field , an area in visual space from which light excites or inhibits the cell.","printedPage":163,"pdfPage":181,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":29},{"text":"The receptive field of a rod or cone is the point in space from which light strikes the cell.","printedPage":163,"pdfPage":181,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":30},{"text":"Everyone on the street reports to a supervisor, whose receptive field is the whole street, the combined area of input.","printedPage":163,"pdfPage":181,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":31},{"text":"All the street supervisors report to the neighborhood manager, whose receptive field is the whole neighborhood.","printedPage":163,"pdfPage":181,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":32},{"text":"Rods and cones with tiny receptive fields connect to a bipolar cell, with a receptive field that combines those of all cells connected to it,","printedPage":163,"pdfPage":181,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":33},{"text":"The receptive fields of ganglion cells converge at the next level, and so on.","printedPage":164,"pdfPage":182,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":34},{"text":"To find a cell’s receptive field, an investigator records from the cell while shining light in various locations.","printedPage":164,"pdfPage":182,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":35},{"text":"If light on a particular spot excites or inhibits the neuron, then that location is part of the neuron’s excitatory or inhibitory receptive field.","printedPage":164,"pdfPage":182,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":36},{"text":"In the simplest case, a ganglion cell’s receptive field has a circular center and an antagonistic doughnutshaped surround.","printedPage":164,"pdfPage":182,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":37},{"text":"The magnocellular neurons, with larger receptive fields, respond to movement and overall patterns, but not color or fine details.","printedPage":165,"pdfPage":183,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":38}],"sourceWordCount":545},{"id":"bp14-m5-2-h04","title":"The Primary goes from the ganglion cells to the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus and then to the primary visual cortex in the occipital cortex, also known","printedPage":165,"pdfPage":183,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":40},{"text":"as area V1 or the striate cortex because of its striped appearance.","printedPage":165,"pdfPage":183,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":41},{"text":"Activity from V1 projects to the frontal cortex, which within 100–200 milliseconds sends information back to modify the activity in V1 and other visual Processing","level":1,"parentId":null,"printedPage":163,"pdfPage":181,"facts":[{"text":"Each cell in the visual system of the brain has a receptive field , an area in visual space from which light excites or inhibits the cell.","printedPage":163,"pdfPage":181,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":29},{"text":"The receptive field of a rod or cone is the point in space from which light strikes the cell.","printedPage":163,"pdfPage":181,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":30},{"text":"Everyone on the street reports to a supervisor, whose receptive field is the whole street, the combined area of input.","printedPage":163,"pdfPage":181,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":31},{"text":"All the street supervisors report to the neighborhood manager, whose receptive field is the whole neighborhood.","printedPage":163,"pdfPage":181,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":32},{"text":"Rods and cones with tiny receptive fields connect to a bipolar cell, with a receptive field that combines those of all cells connected to it,","printedPage":163,"pdfPage":181,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":33},{"text":"The receptive fields of ganglion cells converge at the next level, and so on.","printedPage":164,"pdfPage":182,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":34},{"text":"To find a cell’s receptive field, an investigator records from the cell while shining light in various locations.","printedPage":164,"pdfPage":182,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":35},{"text":"If light on a particular spot excites or inhibits the neuron, then that location is part of the neuron’s excitatory or inhibitory receptive field.","printedPage":164,"pdfPage":182,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":36},{"text":"In the simplest case, a ganglion cell’s receptive field has a circular center and an antagonistic doughnutshaped surround.","printedPage":164,"pdfPage":182,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":37},{"text":"The magnocellular neurons, with larger receptive fields, respond to movement and overall patterns, but not color or fine details.","printedPage":165,"pdfPage":183,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":38},{"text":"Other visual cells derive their receptive fields from the connections they receive.","printedPage":163,"pdfPage":181,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":131},{"text":"For analogy, suppose you keep track of events on a city block.","printedPage":163,"pdfPage":181,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":132},{"text":"Bipolar cells report to a ganglion cell, which therefore has a larger receptive field, as illustrated in Figure 5.17.","printedPage":164,"pdfPage":182,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":133},{"text":"The receptive field might be excited by light in the center and inhibited by light in the surround, or the opposite.","printedPage":164,"pdfPage":182,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":134},{"text":"Some ganglion cells respond only to a stimulus moving in a particular direction.","printedPage":164,"pdfPage":182,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":135},{"text":"(Parvocellular means “small celled,” retina.","printedPage":165,"pdfPage":183,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":136},{"text":"(Magnocellular means “large celled,” from the Latin area V1 or the striate cortex because of its striped appearance.","printedPage":165,"pdfPage":183,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":41},{"text":"Activity from V1 projects to the frontal cortex, which within 100–200 milliseconds sends information back to modify the activity in V1 and other visual areas.","printedPage":165,"pdfPage":183,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":42},{"text":"People with damage in and around area V1 report no conscious of people have no visual imagery at all, other than maybe in a dream now and then.","printedPage":165,"pdfPage":183,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":44},{"text":"People with this condition, called aphantasia , tend to be attracted toward math and science.","printedPage":165,"pdfPage":183,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":45},{"text":"Some people with damage to area V1 display a surprising phenomenon called blindsight , the ability to respond to visual information without perceiving it consciously.","printedPage":165,"pdfPage":183,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":46},{"text":"Many patients respond in one of these ways and not the others, because of differences in which connections were damaged.","printedPage":165,"pdfPage":183,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":47},{"text":"In one study, every patient with blindsight had intact connections from the visual area of the thalamus to the temporal cortex .","printedPage":166,"pdfPage":184,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":48},{"text":"Hyperphantasia is more common among women than men, and it tends to be associated with artistic and other creative occupations.","printedPage":165,"pdfPage":183,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":138},{"text":"When you imagine a visual scene, the activity starts in the memory and language areas of the cortex, and then spreads gradually to V1.","printedPage":165,"pdfPage":183,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":139},{"text":"In any case, the conclusion remains that V1 and surrounding areas are essential for conscious vision.","printedPage":166,"pdfPage":184,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":140},{"text":"Even if your brain is intact, you could experience something like blindsight under certain circumstances.","printedPage":166,"pdfPage":184,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":141}],"originalFacts":9,"additionalFacts":4,"glossary":[{"term":"Lateral activity from cells in cats’ and monkeys’ occipital cortex while they presented visual patterns to the retina.","printedPage":166,"pdfPage":184,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":50},{"text":"The cell had a bar-shaped receptive field, rather than a circular receptive field like cells in the retina and lateral geniculate .","printedPage":166,"pdfPage":184,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":51},{"text":"Light in the excitatory zone increases responses and light in the inhibitory zone decreases it.","printedPage":166,"pdfPage":184,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":52},{"text":"Most simple cells have bar-shaped or edge-shaped receptive fields in horizontal or vertical orientations.","printedPage":166,"pdfPage":184,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":53},{"text":"Most complex cells respond mostly to a stimulus moving in a particular direction—for example, a vertical bar moving left to right.","printedPage":166,"pdfPage":184,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":54},{"text":"The best way to classify a cell as simple or complex is to present a stimulus in several locations.","printedPage":166,"pdfPage":184,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":55},{"text":"A cell that responds to a stimulus in only one location is a simple cell.","printedPage":166,"pdfPage":184,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":56},{"text":"Later researchers found that a cortical cell that responds well to a single bar or line","printedPage":167,"pdfPage":185,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":57},{"text":"Many cortical neurons respond best to a particular spatial frequency of lines and hardly at all to other frequencies .","printedPage":168,"pdfPage":186,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":58},{"text":"How the brain codes vision does not match what we see in any very simple way.","printedPage":168,"pdfPage":186,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":59},{"text":"The illustration shows the receptive field of a simple cell.","printedPage":166,"pdfPage":184,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":142},{"text":"A simple cell has a receptive field with fixed excitatory and inhibitory zones.","printedPage":166,"pdfPage":184,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":143},{"text":"Complex cells, located in areas V1 and V2, also respond to bars and edges, but they respond equally anywhere within a large receptive field.","printedPage":166,"pdfPage":184,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":144},{"text":"An end-stopped or hypercomplex cell resembles a complex cell except that it has a strong inhibitory area at one end of its bar-shaped receptive field.","printedPage":166,"pdfPage":184,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":145},{"text":"From a mathematical standpoint, sine wave frequencies are easy to work with.","printedPage":168,"pdfPage":186,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":146},{"text":"A branch of mathematics called Fourier analysis demonstrates that a combination of sine waves can produce an unlimited variety of other patterns.","printedPage":168,"pdfPage":186,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":147},{"text":"Thus, a series of spatial frequency detectors, some sensitive to horizontal patterns and others to vertical patterns, could represent any possible display.","printedPage":168,"pdfPage":186,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":148},{"text":"Still, we perceive the world as objects, not sine waves.","printedPage":168,"pdfPage":186,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":149}],"originalFacts":10,"additionalFacts":8,"glossary":[{"term":"Receptive the idea of feature detectors is the fact that prolonged exposure to a given visual feature decreases sensitivity to that feature, as if it fatigued the relevant detectors.","printedPage":168,"pdfPage":186,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":63},{"text":"Long ago, Gestalt psychologists rejected the idea that feature detectors tell the whole story about our perceptions.","printedPage":168,"pdfPage":186,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":64},{"text":"It is a top-down process in which other brain areas interpret the visual stimulus and send messages back to reorganize V1 activity.","printedPage":168,"pdfPage":186,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":65},{"text":"In a sense, the brain is constantly forming hypotheses or .","printedPage":168,"pdfPage":186,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":66},{"text":"For example, if you stare at a waterfall for a minute or more and then look away, the rocks and trees next to the waterfall appear to flow upward.","printedPage":168,"pdfPage":186,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":150},{"text":"For example, if you examine Figure 5.22, you might at first see nothing.","printedPage":168,"pdfPage":186,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":151}],"originalFacts":6,"additionalFacts":2,"glossary":[],"sourceBodyWordsAvailable":300,"sourceStatus":"source_explained","mdCrosscheck":"terms_present","wordCount":191},{"id":"bp14-m5-2-h07","title":"Development around.","printedPage":169,"pdfPage":187,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":68},{"text":"Within months, however, you began to recognize faces and crawl visual system develop before birth .","printedPage":169,"pdfPage":187,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":70},{"text":"Waves of spontaneous activity .","printedPage":169,"pdfPage":187,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":71},{"text":"A study of people who were born without eyes found that the .","printedPage":169,"pdfPage":187,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":72},{"text":"Nevertheless, visual experience after birth is necessary for maintaining and modifying the connections.","printedPage":169,"pdfPage":187,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":73},{"text":"Unless you were born blind, .","printedPage":169,"pdfPage":187,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":82},{"text":"If the eyes remain shut still longer, the cortical responses start .","printedPage":169,"pdfPage":187,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":84},{"text":"infant into an older mouse could induce a new period of heightened susceptibility to experience .","printedPage":170,"pdfPage":188,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":85},{"text":"However, even long after the sensitive .","printedPage":170,"pdfPage":188,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":86},{"text":"If neither eye is active, no axon outcompetes any other.","printedPage":169,"pdfPage":187,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":156},{"text":"Eventually, the visual cortex may start responding to auditory or touch stimuli instead.","printedPage":169,"pdfPage":187,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":157},{"text":"Cortical plasticity is greatest in early life, but it never
